brief.head: Gods of the gaps
brief.text: Early hu­mans filled what they could not ex­plain with sun gods and wind gods, Amit Varma said. Some ques­tions stay unan­swered, but that does not make God the an­swer. {083-C05}

brief.head: Four bins for beliefs
brief.text: Ajay Shah sorts be­liefs into four bins, from untestable non­sense to hard knowl­edge. In be­tween sit un­proven work­ing bets: if you hold some, “Welcome aboard.” {083-C03}

brief.head: Armies of the faithful
brief.text: Bands of hunter-gatherers av­er­aged 150 peo­ple, Ajay Shah said. Religion let far big­ger groups fight as fa­nat­ics for an in­vis­i­ble cause, and big­ger armies won. {083-C10}

brief.head: Wired to care
brief.text: Compassion and fam­ily love are gen­uine feel­ings that evolved be­cause they helped our genes spread, Amit Varma said. A self­ish gene does not make us self­ish: “We’re hard­wired to love.” {083-C07}

brief.head: Light, without belief
brief.text: Refusing to cel­e­brate Diwali be­cause you don’t be­lieve in Hinduism makes no sense, Amit Varma said, when fam­ily gath­ers and there is light ev­ery­where. {083-C15}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on life without religion
lead.head: In no God we trust

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 83

body: All over the world, re­li­gios­ity has been going down, Ajay Shah said as he opened the episode. So what hap­pens to peo­ple “when they choose to walk out of the op­er­at­ing sys­tem of re­li­gion”?
Both hosts are athe­ists, and for Amit Varma the sub­ject was per­sonal.
Atheists across the world are frowned upon and even treated with anger, he said. In 13 coun­tries, athe­ism or pub­lic apos­tasy can be pun­ished by death. {#thirteen}
Varma’s own test of so­cial progress is not a woman pres­i­dent of the United States. “What I would love to see is, say, a gay athe­ist in the White House,” he said.
## Not a be­lief

He began with the word. The “ism” in athe­ism sug­gests a be­lief sys­tem, Varma said, and so peo­ple as­sume that athe­ists be­lieve there is no God. “The cor­rect def­i­ni­tion in­volves not be­lief but an ab­sence of be­lief.” {083-C01}

No one has proved to him that God ex­ists, any more than pink fairies, so he be­lieves in nei­ther. “I be­lieve that there is no God” claims a false cer­tainty, he ar­gued, since no one can prove a neg­a­tive.
The bur­den of proof lies with who­ever makes the claim. If any­one proved that God ex­ists, Varma said, he would be­come a be­liever: “I’m a ra­tio­nal­ist. I go by the proof.”
Nor is an ag­nos­tic a fence-sitter be­tween be­liever and athe­ist. Atheism is about be­lief and ag­nos­ti­cism about knowl­edge, Varma said, and he is both an athe­ist and an ag­nos­tic.
## What faith was for

None of this de­nies religion’s past. It has played “a su­perbly im­por­tant role through human his­tory”, Varma said, and he listed the four func­tions it has served: ex­pla­na­tion, mean­ing, moral­ity and con­so­la­tion.
Science has filled most of the gaps that gods once ex­plained. Meaning, he ar­gued, has to come from re­al­ity, not from “man­u­fac­tured fic­tion”. {083-C04}
Morality, in his ac­count, came be­fore re­li­gion. Evolution wired in com­pas­sion, liv­ing to­gether pro­duced norms, and re­li­gion ar­rived last to cod­ify them.
Consolation in the face of death was the one job he con­ceded. Still, he would not be­lieve in a fic­tion to con­sole him­self. “Grief is grief,” he said.
## Faith in re­treat

Shah took the long view. Household sur­veys show re­li­gios­ity de­clin­ing all over the world: first in Western Europe after the Second World War, and over the last 25 years in the United States as well.

His ex­pla­na­tion is that every re­li­gion looks strange to those not raised in it. Faith that is not “dinned into your head as a child” rarely takes, so a fam­ily that leaves does not re­turn. “So it’s like once it’s gone, it can never come back.” {083-C12}
Conformity speeds the process. When most peo­ple are re­li­gious, the rest go along; once be­lief falls below a crit­i­cal mass, peo­ple start say­ing openly that they don’t care.
Shah sug­gested that, with right-wing re­li­gious na­tion­al­ism on the rise, harm­ful old be­liefs may need call­ing out more firmly.
Varma ended with three ex­hor­ta­tions: be­ware the new sec­u­lar re­li­gions, keep the tra­di­tions that bring peo­ple to­gether, and never im­pose your be­liefs on any­one.

Atheists who mock be­liev­ers be­have badly too, he said, and many of his friends are re­li­gious. “I think the great­est re­li­gion is to treat other human be­ings as ac­tual peo­ple and not as means to an end.” {083-C16}

second.label: Defining atheism
second.head: No stamps, no church
second.deck: Amit Varma reads out a reader’s letter to The Economist in full

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the letter from Ottawa

body: In 2007, when Amit Varma wrote the first of his col­umns on athe­ism, *The Economist* had called athe­ism a new re­li­gion. A reader, Chad English of Ottawa, wrote in to protest, and Varma read his let­ter out in full. {#economist}

Why don’t athe­ists or­gan­ise or wield in­flu­ence? “The an­swer is easy,” English wrote. “Atheism is a re­li­gion in the same way that not col­lect­ing stamps is a hobby.” A gov­ern­ment that pushed laws favour­ing stamp col­lect­ing would be a bad gov­ern­ment, he added, and the same is true of a re­li­gious one.
Then the sign-off: “See you at the next non-meeting.” Varma bor­rows the com­par­i­son when­ever some­one calls athe­ism an­other re­li­gion or a be­lief sys­tem. {083-S02}

quote.text: Atheism is no more a re­li­gion than not col­lect­ing stamps is a hobby.

third.head: Survival of the cutest

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the stories that stuck

body: Why did the sun god and the wind god last? Ajay Shah passed on an in­sight from Ashok Desai, who told him that the human mind came first. {#desai}

In the oral tra­di­tion, Desai said, peo­ple kept in­vent­ing and mu­tat­ing sto­ries. The fan­ci­ful ones that were cute and in­ter­est­ing to the human mind stuck; the ones that clicked in­side the brain were re­mem­bered.

Shah gave the idea a mod­ern form. “There are fifty thou­sand sub­red­dits about the mur­der of JFK, and a cou­ple of them gain promi­nence be­cause they just fit in the human mind bet­ter.” {083-S05}
On this ac­count, the sto­ries that sur­vive are those that fit the mind best. Shah of­fered it in re­sponse to Amit Varma’s ac­count of the gods of the gaps.

box.text: Richard Dawkins wrote *The Selfish Gene*, which Amit Varma says is widely mis­read: self­ish genes make us lov­ing, not self­ish. He also wrote *The God Delusion*, and pointed out that every be­liever is an athe­ist about all the other re­li­gions. {083-C11}

sections.label: The definition
sections.head: Absence makes the case
sections.caption: atheism as an absence of belief
body: Atheism is mis­un­der­stood by many peo­ple, Amit Varma said, and he wanted to de­fine it first. The trou­ble be­gins with the word. Its “ism” sug­gests a be­lief sys­tem, so peo­ple think of athe­ists as peo­ple who be­lieve that there is no God.
That, he said, is not the cor­rect def­i­ni­tion. “The cor­rect def­i­ni­tion in­volves not be­lief but an ab­sence of be­lief.” {083-C01}

No one has proved to him that God ex­ists, so he does not be­lieve in God, just as he does not be­lieve in pink fairies. “I be­lieve that there is no God” claims a false cer­tainty, he said, be­cause no one can prove a neg­a­tive. “I don’t be­lieve that there is God” is in an en­tirely dif­fer­ent cat­e­gory.
## The bur­den of proof
The bur­den of proof lies with the per­son who says “I be­lieve X”, Varma said, not with him. If some­one proved to­mor­row that God ex­ists, he would be­come a be­liever: he goes by the proof.

Nor is athe­ism an ac­tiv­ity. “It is a pas­sive thing,” he said. A reader’s let­ter to *The Economist*, from around the time of Varma’s first col­umns on athe­ism in 2007, made the point with stamps. {#economist}
~ Varma is not mil­i­tant about it. Many of his friends are re­li­gious, and that is per­fectly fine with him: “Let’s not im­pose on each other.”

quote.text: If some­one were to hy­po­thet­i­cally prove to­mor­row that God does exist, then I will be a be­liever be­cause I’m a ra­tio­nal­ist.

sections.label: Two questions
sections.head: Knowing is not believing
sections.caption: belief, knowledge and four bins
body: People pic­ture be­lief as a line, Amit Varma said: the be­liever at one end, the athe­ist at the other, and the un­de­cided ag­nos­tic in the mid­dle. That is not true. “Atheism is about be­lief. Agnostic is about knowl­edge.” {083-C02}
The root of ag­nos­tic is *gnosis*, knowl­edge. An ag­nos­tic holds that the truth about God can never be known. So a be­liever can be an ag­nos­tic, and so, like Varma, can an athe­ist.
## Four bins
Ajay Shah con­nected this to Karl Popper. A the­ory is in­ter­est­ing and worth con­sid­er­ing, he said, when it makes pre­dic­tions that are vul­ner­a­ble to fal­si­fi­ca­tion. {083-R12}

From that he built a set of bins. At one edge sits fan­ci­ful non­sense like Erich von Däniken’s *Chariots of the Gods*, which Shah read as a child and which “just doesn’t make a sin­gle testable propo­si­tion”. {083-J10} At the other is hard knowl­edge such as evo­lu­tion­ary bi­ol­ogy. In be­tween are work­ing bets that fu­ture ev­i­dence may set­tle, and be­liefs held be­cause of so­cial pro­gram­ming, peer pres­sure or con­ve­nience.

~ Everybody holds be­liefs of that last kind, Shah said, and it would be good to be self-aware about them. As for the mid­dle zone: “So, gen­tle reader, if you’re em­bar­rassed to be­lieve some things that you’re not yet ready to prove, great. Welcome aboard.” {083-C03}

quote.text: Equally, like me, you can be an athe­ist and an ag­nos­tic at the same time.

sections.label: What religion does
sections.head: Four jobs, one vacancy
sections.caption: the four jobs religion does
body: Atheists are often asked what could re­place re­li­gion, Amit Varma said. He named four func­tions it per­forms, and con­fessed that for one of them he had no con­vinc­ing an­swer. {#functions}

The first is ex­pla­na­tion. Early hu­mans made up a sun god and a wind god, and as knowl­edge filled the gaps, those gods of the gaps van­ished. Varma read out Douglas Adams: “I take the awe of un­der­stand­ing over the awe of ig­no­rance any day.” {083-J07}
The sec­ond is mean­ing, which must come from re­al­ity, he said, or it would be “fake and shal­low”.
## Goodness be­fore God

The third is moral­ity. Evolution wired in com­pas­sion and care for kin, liv­ing to­gether pro­duced norms such as not steal­ing, and re­li­gion came last to cod­ify them. “First we have the hard­wiring, then peo­ple live to­gether, then you have the norms, then re­li­gion kind of cod­i­fies it.” {083-C06}

Reason does the rest. Plato’s Euthyphro dilemma asks whether some­thing is good be­cause God wills it, or whether God wills it be­cause it is good; ei­ther way, moral­ity does not de­pend on God. {083-C08} Kant, Bentham and Mill, and Aristotle each reached ethics with­out re­li­gion.
~ The fourth is con­so­la­tion in the face of death, and there Varma con­cedes ground. “I can’t help being an athe­ist,” he said. {083-S03}

quote.text: God could go mad one day and will any damn thing and we have to do it.

sections.label: New atheism
sections.head: When atheism got loud
sections.caption: the Four Horsemen of new atheism
body: The athe­ism Ajay Shah and Amit Varma grew up with was per­sonal and be­nign. Shah’s fa­ther was an athe­ist who blended eas­ily into a re­li­gious so­ci­ety. But Shah sees a more hawk­ish athe­is­tic cul­ture shap­ing up.

About twenty years ago, Varma said, a group of peo­ple came to be­lieve, “if I may say so with good rea­son”, that re­li­gion is a root cause of much evil in the world, and that they must speak out. {#twentyyears}

They be­came the Four Horsemen: Richard Dawkins, au­thor of *The God Delusion*; Sam Harris, au­thor of *The End of Faith*; Daniel Dennett; and Christopher Hitchens, whom Varma adored and still misses. {083-R03}

Dawkins called the God of the Old Testament “ar­guably the most un­pleas­ant char­ac­ter in all fic­tion”. {#oldtestament} He also pointed out that every be­liever is an athe­ist about all the other re­li­gions. {083-C11}
## A move­ment played out

The irony, Varma said, is that their as­sertive­ness made athe­ism look like just an­other com­pet­ing be­lief sys­tem. He agrees with many of their cri­tiques of or­gan­ised re­li­gion and dogma, but feels re­li­gions en­code tra­di­tions that exist for a rea­son.
~ The move­ment has played it­self out, he said. Two of the four horse­men, Dennett and Hitchens, are dead, and Dawkins is in his eight­ies. {#twodead}

quote.text: Dawkins beau­ti­fully pointed out that ac­tu­ally every be­liever is an athe­ist be­cause you be­lieve in your one re­li­gion.

sections.label: Faith in decline
sections.head: Below the critical mass
sections.caption: why religiosity keeps falling
body: Household sur­veys show re­li­gios­ity fall­ing world­wide, Ajay Shah said. In Western Europe it fell after the Second World War. As the fa­mous quote goes, “After Auschwitz, there can be no art”; after it, faith in a be­nign, all-powerful God was hard to hold. {083-J09}
In the United States it held up for a while, then col­lapsed over the last 25 years.
Shah’s rea­son the de­cline is ir­re­versible: to any­one not raised in a faith, its be­liefs sound weird. Once a fam­ily stops pass­ing faith on, he said, “it can never come back”. {083-C12}
## Tipping points

Conformity mat­ters too. When re­li­gios­ity was 60, 70, 80 per cent, peo­ple had a strong rea­son to go along; below some crit­i­cal mass, they start say­ing openly that they don’t care, and the de­cline ac­cel­er­ates. {#critical}

Amit Varma re­called Hannah Arendt’s “ba­nal­ity of evil”: or­di­nary peo­ple can show the great­est cru­elty, and nei­ther re­li­gion nor ra­tio­nal­ity guards against it. Prosperity, he sug­gested, makes it least likely: “per­haps the best an­swer to get to the kind of moral­ity we would all like is a ris­ing GDP”. {083-C13}

~ Shah of­fered a coun­terex­am­ple: Nazi Germany, “the land of Albert Einstein and Beethoven”. {#einstein} Varma replied that it rose from the ruins of the First World War, with­out which he doubted Hitler would have come to power.

quote.text: My sis­ters and I have zero. Their kids have zero.

art.caption: Amit Varma on why religiosity keeps falling

sections.label: Closing thoughts
sections.head: Keep the lamps, drop the dogma
sections.caption: keeping tradition without dogma
body: Amit Varma closed with three ex­hor­ta­tions. The first: or­gan­ised re­li­gion is de­clin­ing, but the in­stinct to choose a be­lief sys­tem is still there, in new re­li­gions from Marxism to wokeism, each with its own dogma and in­tol­er­ance.

Question any part of the woke dogma, he said, and you are an out­cast; sup­port an out­cast and you be­come one too. It re­minded him of Pakistan’s blas­phemy law: “And tur­tles all the way down.” {083-J11}
Anyone who ac­cepts an ide­o­log­i­cal tribe’s en­tire pack­age, Varma said, is not think­ing in­de­pen­dently. {083-C14}
## Baby and bath­wa­ter

The sec­ond: don’t throw the baby out with the bath­wa­ter. Traditions give com­fort and com­mu­nity. As for re­fus­ing to cel­e­brate Diwali be­cause you don’t be­lieve in Hinduism, he sees no sense in it. “You don’t need to be­lieve in God to cel­e­brate a tra­di­tion like that.” {083-C15}
Keep away the re­gres­sive, misog­y­nis­tic cus­toms, he said, em­brace the life-affirming ones, and never co­erce any­one.
~ The third: whether you are re­li­gious or an athe­ist, don’t im­pose your be­liefs on oth­ers. Atheists who mock be­liev­ers be­have badly too. {083-C16}

quote.text: But there are some things that can be life af­firm­ing, that can bring you closer to your fel­low peo­ple, em­brace them.

So when­ever any­one con­forms to the en­tire be­lief pack­age of some ide­o­log­i­cal tribe, I know they’re not think­ing in­de­pen­dently for them­selves. And they might just be a de­vout bhakta of what­ever ide­o­log­i­cal tribe that is.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Spaghetti, grief, a father’s exit and a teenage detour, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the gentlest way to protest religion
stories.head: Hands off my spaghetti
body: Amit Varma’s favourite protest against re­li­gion is a be­nign one, and it started in Kansas. In 2005, the Kansas School Board was try­ing to teach cre­ation­ism, and a gen­tle­man named Bobby Henderson wrote it a let­ter. {#kansas}
If the board was going to treat all be­liefs equally, Henderson ar­gued, it would have to treat his too. He be­lieved in Pastafarianism, whose fol­low­ers wor­ship the Flying Spaghetti Monster.
And if other re­li­gions were not to be of­fended, Varma said, voic­ing Henderson, then nei­ther was he: “The Flying Spaghetti Monster is my God. I’m a proud Pastafarian.”
Around 2007, Varma took up Henderson’s cre­ation in a col­umn about free speech called *Don’t Insult Pasta*. He, too, de­clared him­self a Pastafarian. {083-S04}
The satir­i­cal point was sim­ple. “If you don’t want me to of­fend your God, don’t of­fend mine,” he said. “Say noth­ing about pasta.”

It was all tongue in cheek, Varma added, be­fore swerv­ing into diet ad­vice. Pasta is carbs, he warned, and read­ers should eat a lot of meat, some fat and not much carb. Pasta is evil, ex­cept once in a while. {083-J03}
Even here he would not lay down the law. He was not going to be dog­matic about it, he said, be­cause good athe­ists are not dog­matic.

~ He likes this tongue-in-cheek way of doing things, he said, be­cause it makes the ab­sur­dity of oth­ers vis­i­ble. It is gen­tler than the new athe­ists, who spoke out against re­li­gion very strongly.
stories.why: Demands for spe­cial treat­ment, and for be­liefs never to be of­fended, look ar­bi­trary once any­one can found a faith. Gentle satire ex­poses that with­out hos­til­ity, which is why Varma prefers it to the as­sertive­ness of new athe­ism. {083-R11}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Flying Spaghetti Monster

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the one thing reason cannot give
stories.head: Comfort he would not fake
body: Amit Varma’s mother died in 2007. The next year he wrote a col­umn in *Mail Today* called *What’s Consolation for an Atheist?* {083-R08}

It took on the one func­tion of re­li­gion he ad­mits he can­not re­place. Explanation, mean­ing and moral­ity can come from sci­ence and rea­son, he ar­gued, but mor­tal­ity is hard to deal with, and on con­so­la­tion he has no an­swer.
The con­clu­sion he reached then still holds. “I can’t help being an athe­ist. I’m not going to start be­liev­ing in a fic­tion be­cause I need to con­sole my­self.” {083-S03}

~ Varma doubts re­li­gion of­fers much com­fort ei­ther. “Ultimately be­reave­ment is be­reave­ment, grief is grief,” he said. If he con­cedes any ground to re­li­gion, it is here, “but then I don’t have an op­tion”.
stories.why: Intellectual hon­esty can cost com­fort. Rather than pre­tend that rea­son solves ev­ery­thing, Varma openly gives up this one piece of ground to re­li­gion, and still de­clines to be­lieve in a con­sol­ing fic­tion.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on consolation for an atheist

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a family that left religion for good
stories.head: The family that never went back
body: As a young per­son, Ajay Shah’s fa­ther had a deep com­mit­ment to Hinduism and a deep knowl­edge of it. As an adult, he be­came an athe­ist. {083-S06}
His athe­ism was re­laxed. “My fa­ther was athe­ist, but it was never un­com­fort­able,” Shah said. He blended per­fectly into a so­ci­ety with many re­li­gious peo­ple, as Shah does today.
After the switch, re­li­gion van­ished from the fam­ily. “My sis­ters and I have zero. Their kids have zero.” And, Shah said, “once it’s gone, it can never come back”. {083-C12}

~ Shah told the story while ex­plain­ing why re­li­gios­ity is fall­ing world­wide. To any­one not raised in a faith, he said, its be­liefs sound weird, just as the Christians’ be­liefs would to some­one raised a Buddhist.
stories.why: The story is Shah’s larger the­sis in minia­ture. Belief that is not in­stilled in child­hood rarely re­turns, he ar­gues, so a fam­ily that leaves re­li­gion stays out, and the de­cline of re­li­gios­ity runs in one di­rec­tion.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father’s exit from Hinduism

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how he reasoned his way out
stories.head: The spirit was willing, briefly
body: Amit Varma says he was al­ways an athe­ist. But there was a vague time in his teens, when he was “very im­ma­ture”, when he held that spir­i­tu­al­ity was dif­fer­ent from re­li­gion.
In that phase he be­lieved there was “some vast un­know­able pres­ence which gov­erns us all”. Then, he said, “I was soon dis­abused of that no­tion by life and ra­tio­nal­ity.” {083-S01}
Many peo­ple turn to athe­ism as an act of re­bel­lion against con­ven­tion. Varma said he did not re­ally do that, though it might have been part of the story.

~ He began to think about athe­ism se­ri­ously only as an adult, and ar­rived at his def­i­ni­tion of it over a long pe­riod. That def­i­ni­tion, an ab­sence of be­lief rather than a be­lief, be­came the start­ing point of the episode. {083-C01}
stories.why: Disbelief can be rea­soned into slowly rather than seized in a sin­gle act of re­bel­lion. For Varma, a spir­i­tu­al­ity dis­tinct from re­li­gion was a half­way house he soon left be­hind.

overheard.text: Gentle read­ers, please have a lot of meat, some fat, not much carb, pasta is evil.
overheard.who: Amit Varma, mid-Pastafarianism, swerving into diet advice

quiz.q: In Chad English’s letter, atheism is a religion in the same way as what?
quiz.a: The way not col­lect­ing stamps is a hobby: athe­ists don’t con­gre­gate.

quiz.q: Atheism is about belief, said Amit Varma. What is agnosticism about, and what is its root?
quiz.a: Knowledge: from gno­sis, it holds the truth about God can never be known.

quiz.q: Which of Plato’s puzzles asks whether something is good because God wills it?
quiz.a: The Euthyphro dilemma: ei­ther way, moral­ity does not de­pend on God.

quiz.q: Of religion’s four functions, which one did Varma concede reason cannot replace?
quiz.a: Consolation in the face of death; grief, he said, is grief.

quiz.q: What average group size did Ajay Shah give for bands of hunter-gatherers?
quiz.a: An av­er­age of 150, be­fore re­li­gion let far big­ger groups fight as fa­nat­ics.

quiz.q: In 2005, what did Bobby Henderson ask the Kansas School Board to respect equally?
quiz.a: His faith, Pastafarianism, whose god is the Flying Spaghetti Monster.

glossary.def: A devo­tee; Varma’s word for an ide­o­log­i­cal tribe’s faith­ful fol­lower
One who holds the truth about God can never be known
Popper’s test: a the­ory worth con­sid­er­ing makes pre­dic­tions that could fail
Being good to oth­ers be­cause it serves the in­ter­est of our genes

Abandoning one’s re­li­gion; pun­ish­able by death in 13 coun­tries

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 83. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); Karl Popper (Franz Barta, No restrictions); Hannah Arendt (Wikimedia Commons, public domain).

shelf.title: The Moral Animal
shelf.creator: Robert Wright
shelf.why: Amit’s pick among books on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion be­cause it deals with moral­ity: how evo­lu­tion pro­duced our bet­ter in­stincts (it taught him ‘re­cip­ro­cal altruism’) and how mar­riage evolved, with monogamy and polygamy as adap­ta­tions to dif­fer­ent cir­cum­stances.

shelf.title: The Selfish Gene
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s metaphor of the self­ish gene which, read care­fully rather than lit­er­ally, ex­plains why hu­mans are ca­pa­ble of love and al­tru­ism.

shelf.title: The God Delusion
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s case against or­gan­ised re­li­gion and dogma, which Amit thinks de­serves to be taken se­ri­ously even though his own athe­ism is gen­tler.

shelf.title: The End of Faith
shelf.creator: Sam Harris
shelf.why: One of the found­ing New Atheist books whose cri­tiques of or­gan­ised re­li­gion Amit says you have to take se­ri­ously.

shelf.title: Sam Harris’s conversation podcast
shelf.creator: Sam Harris
shelf.why: Sam Harris’s con­ver­sa­tion pod­cast, which Amit rec­om­mends for the art of con­ver­sa­tion: he learned a lot about pod­cast­ing from its flow and rhythm in the early days, though it is now mostly pay­walled and Harris has moved in dif­fer­ent di­rec­tions.

shelf.title: Christopher Hitchens’s writing
shelf.creator: Christopher Hitchens
shelf.why: Amit says he adored Hitchens and misses him.

shelf.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
shelf.creator: Hannah Arendt
shelf.why: It is a warn­ing that or­di­nary peo­ple can com­mit ex­tra­or­di­nary cru­elty, and that nei­ther re­li­gion nor ra­tio­nal­ity pro­tects against it.

shelf.title: What’s Consolation for an Atheist?
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is where he takes on the one func­tion of re­li­gion he can’t re­place, con­so­la­tion in grief, and de­cides he won’t adopt a com­fort­ing fic­tion.

shelf.title: Don’t Insult Pasta
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A play­ful satire on de­mands not to of­fend re­li­gious sen­ti­ment (if you don’t want me to of­fend your god, don’t of­fend mine), part of Amit’s two decades of col­umns on free speech in India.

shelf.title: A Godless Congregation
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Further read­ing from Amit’s own writ­ing on athe­ism over the years.

shelf.title: Flying Spaghetti Monster
shelf.creator: Bobby Henderson
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite ex­am­ple of the be­nign, tongue-in-cheek way to protest re­li­gion, by show­ing how ab­surd it is to de­mand spe­cial treat­ment for be­liefs.

shelf.title: Falsifiability
shelf.creator: Karl Popper
shelf.why: He finds it a lovely or­gan­is­ing prin­ci­ple.

shelf.title: The Euthyphro Dilemma
shelf.creator: Plato
shelf.why: It shows that even if God ex­ists, moral­ity can­not sim­ply come from di­vine com­mand.

shelf.title: The Categorical Imperative
shelf.creator: Immanuel Kant
shelf.why: He finds the for­mu­la­tion ‘treat peo­ple as ends in them­selves, not as means to an end’ in­cred­i­bly deep and beau­ti­ful.

shelf.title: Utilitarianism
shelf.creator: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
shelf.why: He thinks it is sound on the whole and worth know­ing, but cri­tiques it with Hayek’s knowl­edge prob­lem: the world is too com­plex to know the con­se­quences of our ac­tions.

shelf.title: Virtue Ethics
shelf.creator: Aristotle
shelf.why: It ap­peals to him be­cause it iden­ti­fies ways of be­hav­ing that make ev­ery­body bet­ter off and lead to human pros­per­ity, with­out need­ing re­li­gion.

laughs.text: Amit isn’t im­pressed by talk of a fu­ture woman US pres­i­dent, since Hillary Clinton al­ready won the pop­u­lar vote in 2016. His real bench­mark: ‘what I would love to see is, say, a gay athe­ist in the White House. You know, that’ll be the day when I’ll say so­ci­ety has re­ally pro­gressed.’
Chad English’s let­ter to The Economist, read by Amit: ‘Atheism is a re­li­gion in the same way that not col­lect­ing stamps is a hobby... See you at the next non-meeting.’

Ajay on Kant: ‘hear no evil, see no evil, do no evil, and you will never write a best­seller... never use an­other human being as an in­stru­ment and you prob­a­bly won’t gain a lot of power.’ Amit: ‘Shame shame, how can you say such a thing?’

Humanists International finds that athe­ism or pub­lic apos­tasy can be pun­ished by death in 13 coun­tries, and that most of the UN’s 193 mem­ber states per­se­cute athe­ism in some form, for in­stance through blas­phemy laws.

Richard Dawkins on the God of the Old Testament, read out by Amit: ‘ar­guably the most un­pleas­ant char­ac­ter in all fic­tion... a vin­dic­tive, blood­thirsty eth­nic cleanser; a misog­y­nis­tic, ho­mo­pho­bic, racist, in­fan­ti­ci­dal, geno­ci­dal, fil­i­ci­dal, pesti­len­tial, mega­lo­ma­ni­a­cal, sado­masochis­tic, capri­ciously malev­o­lent bully.’

Austin Cline, quoted by Amit: a per­son who truly en­joys their life will do so re­gard­less of whether any af­ter­life ex­ists, and ‘won’t de­pend upon the ex­is­tence of such a heaven in order for their lives to have mean­ing or pur­pose.’
Ajay in­vokes ‘the fa­mous quote’ ‘After Auschwitz, there can be no art’ to ex­plain why, after the war, Western Europeans found it hard to be­lieve in a be­nign, all-powerful God.

Ajay’s child­hood read, Erich von Däniken’s Chariots of the Gods, which he calls ‘ob­scure nonsense’: a fan­ci­ful story of be­ings from outer space start­ing life on Earth that ‘just doesn’t make a sin­gle testable proposition’.

Amit com­pares wokeism’s can­cel­la­tions to Pakistan’s blas­phemy law, under which de­fend­ing the ac­cused makes you a blas­phe­mer too: ‘And tur­tles all the way down.’ He cites what hap­pened to J.K. Rowling.
Amit sets the scene for why re­li­gion arose by de­scrib­ing the pre-scientific world as ‘na­ture red in tooth and claw’, where ‘life is nasty, brutish, and short’.
